concept.name: Observability Golden Signals

relationships.description: Connects Observability Golden Signals to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: The Four Golden Signals—Latency, Traffic, Errors, and Saturation—form the minimal, high-signal metric foundation for monitoring any user-facing distributed system. Measuring them with histograms (not averages) and separating successful vs. failed request latencies exposes tail regressions and capacity cliffs before outages hit.
spark.keyTakeaway: Instrument every service boundary with Prometheus/OTel histograms for Latency (p50/p95/p99, splitting 2xx from 5xx), Traffic (RPS), Errors (explicit + policy), and Saturation (the tightest resource bottleneck)—and alert on SLO error-budget burn rates rather than raw CPU spikes.

concept.whyItMatters: Dashboards crammed with 80 infrastructure graphs hide the few symptoms users actually feel. The Four Golden Signals (from Google's SRE handbook) give on-call engineers an immediate triage framework: if you can only measure four things on a service, measure these four.
whenToUse: Designing baseline SLIs, SLOs, and executive health dashboards for any HTTP, gRPC, or streaming microservice.
Triaging live incidents to isolate whether degradation stems from downstream latency, traffic surges, code errors, or resource exhaustion.
Building multi-window, multi-burn-rate SLO alerts that page humans only when user-facing error budgets are genuinely threatened.
whenNotToUse: Debugging a single user's failed request or pinpointing which line of code threw an exception—use distributed traces and structured logs for root cause.
Monitoring offline batch/ETL jobs where throughput, queue age, and completion freshness matter more than interactive request latency.
Replacing business KPIs (checkout conversion, payment authorization rate), which complement technical signals.
keyPoints: **Latency**: Track request duration using histograms (e.g., `http_server_request_duration_seconds`) and report p50, p95, and p99—never averages, which mask 10-second tail stalls. Always separate fast-failing `5xx` error latency from successful `2xx` latency.
**Traffic**: Measure demand in domain-appropriate units—requests per second (RPS) for APIs, messages/sec for Kafka consumers, or active concurrent sessions for WebSockets.
**Errors**: Capture explicit failures (`5xx`, uncaught exceptions), implicit failures (`200 OK` with an empty or stale payload), and policy failures (rate-limit `429` or SLA violations > 1,000ms).
**Saturation**: Measure how full your most constrained resource is *before* it hits 100%—thread pool utilization, DB connection pool wait queue, JVM heap after GC, or CPU CFS throttling.
Pair the Golden Signals with **USE** (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) for hardware/infrastructure and **RED** (Rate, Errors, Duration) for request-driven microservices.

examples.title: Separating 5xx Error Latency Exposes Hidden Checkout Stall
examples.scenario: A checkout API's blended p99 latency dropped from 240ms to 90ms during an outage, confusing on-call engineers because a broken Redis connection was failing fast in 2ms with `500` errors.
examples.outcome: Splitting `histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)` by `status_class="2xx"` vs. `"5xx"` immediately revealed that `2xx` p99 had actually spiked to 1,800ms on fallback DB queries while `5xx` fast-fails skewed the blended curve.

examples.title: Catching Connection Pool Saturation Before 503 Outage
examples.scenario: Service CPU sat at a healthy 35%, yet every afternoon at peak traffic the API started timing out.
examples.outcome: Tracking HikariCP `hikaricp_connections_pending` (Saturation) showed the 20-connection DB pool hitting 100% utilization and queuing threads 15 minutes before `504` errors appeared, prompting pool sizing and slow-query tuning.

tradeOffs.factor: Native Histograms vs. Fixed Bucket Histograms
tradeOffs.pro: Fixed Prometheus buckets (`le="0.1", "0.25", "0.5", "1.0"`) are universally supported, while OTel exponential/native histograms preserve accurate p99 across shifting scales without manual bucket tuning.
tradeOffs.con: Over-specified fixed buckets (`20+` buckets x high-cardinality labels) multiply time-series cardinality by 20x.

tradeOffs.factor: Symptom-Based SLO Alerts vs. Cause-Based Resource Alerts
tradeOffs.pro: Alerting on Golden Signal SLO burn rate (Latency + Errors) cuts false-positive pages by 70%+ because high CPU without latency/error impact doesn't wake engineers.
tradeOffs.con: Rapidly growing saturation (e.g., disk filling at 92%) still needs a proactive warning ticket before it causes an abrupt 100% error cliff.

tradeOffs.pro: Server-side metrics are cheap and always available, while client/synthetic RUM metrics capture DNS, TLS, and CDN latency invisible to origin pods.
tradeOffs.con: Client-side telemetry is noisy across user networks and cannot observe internal microservice saturation.

failureModes.name: Averaging Latency Hides Tail Outages
failureModes.description: Reporting `avg(duration)` shows 45ms even when 2% of requests (all mobile checkouts) time out at 10,000ms.
failureModes.mitigation: Export HDR/Prometheus histograms and compute `histogram_quantile(0.95, ...)` and `0.99` over `rate(...[5m])`.

failureModes.name: Silent 200 OK Implicit Errors
failureModes.description: A degraded recommendation engine returns `HTTP 200` with an empty JSON array `[]`; `5xx` error rate stays at `0.0%` while conversion plummets.
failureModes.mitigation: Emit explicit domain error/fallback counters (`recommendation_fallback_total{reason="timeout"}`) and include them in the service's Error SLI.

failureModes.name: High-Cardinality Label Explosion
failureModes.description: Adding `user_id`, `request_id`, or unnormalized URL paths (`/users/12345`) to Golden Signal metrics crashes Prometheus/Mimir.
failureModes.mitigation: Restrict metric labels to bounded dimensions (`service`, `route_template`, `method`, `status_class`); keep `user_id` and `trace_id` in traces/logs or exemplars.

failureModes.name: Averaging Across Multi-Pod Saturation
failureModes.description: Alerting on cluster-wide average CPU (40%) misses one hot shard or single-threaded Node.js/Python worker pinned at 100% CPU.
failureModes.mitigation: Aggregate saturation using `max()` or `p99()` across pods (`max(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total)`) rather than cluster `avg()`.

commonMistakes: Computing client-side quantiles (`Summary` metrics) on individual pods and then averaging them across pods in Grafana—quantiles cannot be averaged mathematically.
Grouping `4xx` client typos (`404`, `400`) into server error alerts, causing noisy pages whenever a bot scrapes invalid URLs.
Using CPU utilization as the sole Saturation metric while ignoring memory pressure, disk IOPS, Kafka consumer lag, and thread/connection pool queues.
Setting static thresholds (`latency > 200ms for 1m`) instead of multi-window SLO burn-rate alerts (`14.4x` burn over 5m/1h).
Missing Prometheus **exemplars** on latency histograms, forcing engineers to hunt manually for a `trace_id` during a p99 spike.

sections.content:
## The idea

Coined in Google's *Site Reliability Engineering* book, the **Four Golden Signals** define the essential telemetry needed to understand user experience and system headroom: **Latency**, **Traffic**, **Errors**, and **Saturation**.

Instead of building dashboards around arbitrary internal counters, Golden Signals organize monitoring around **external symptoms** (Latency, Traffic, Errors) and **leading capacity indicators** (Saturation). When Latency or Errors degrade, Traffic and Saturation immediately tell you *why*—whether a sudden 3x traffic spike pushed the database pool to 100% saturation, or a bad deploy introduced `500` errors at flat traffic.

## Concrete walkthrough

Here is how a payment API instrumented with **OpenTelemetry** and **Prometheus** exposes and correlates all four signals during a flash sale:

1. **Traffic**: `sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service="payments"}[1m]))` jumps from 1,200 RPS to 4,800 RPS.
2. **Saturation**: `max(hikaricp_connections_active / hikaricp_connections_max)` hits `1.0` (100%), and `hikaricp_connections_pending` climbs from 0 to 140 queued threads.
3. **Latency**: `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket{status_class="2xx"}[2m])))` degrades from 45ms to 1,400ms as threads wait for DB connections.
4. **Errors**: Requests exceeding the 2,000ms gateway timeout fail with `504`; `sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{status_class="5xx"}[1m])) / sum(rate(...[1m]))` crosses 2.5%, triggering a fast-burn SLO page with a linked Grafana **exemplar** `trace_id` pointing straight to `hikaricp.acquire`.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Mapping Golden Signals to RED and USE
sections.content:
## Mapping Golden Signals to RED and USE

Two popular mnemonics operationalize the Four Golden Signals depending on the layer:

- **RED Method (Request-driven services)**: **R**ate (Traffic), **E**rrors, **D**uration (Latency). Ideal for microservices, API gateways, and serverless functions. It omits Saturation because container orchestrators often surface saturation separately.
- **USE Method (Infrastructure resources)**: **U**tilization (% busy), **S**aturation (queue depth/throttling), **E**rrors (hardware/dropped packets). Ideal for CPUs, NVMe disks, network interfaces, Kubernetes nodes, and DB connection pools.

Together, **RED + Saturation** gives you the complete Four Golden Signals.

## Golden Signals reference specification

| Signal | What to Measure | Preferred Metric Type | Key Pitfall to Avoid |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Latency** | `p50`, `p95`, `p99` request duration (`2xx` vs `5xx`) | Histogram / Native Histogram | Averaging latency or mixing fast `5xx` errors with `2xx` |
| **Traffic** | RPS, Kafka msgs/sec, active streams | Counter (`rate()`) | Counting health-check `/healthz` pings in user traffic |
| **Errors** | `5xx`, policy rejections, silent fallbacks | Counter (`rate()` ratio) | Paging on client `404`s or ignoring `200` empty responses |
| **Saturation** | Pool queue depth, CFS CPU throttle, lag | Gauge / Histogram | Watching cluster-wide avg CPU instead of `max()` per pod |

## Failure modes

**1. Low-Traffic Alert Flapping**: At 2 AM when traffic drops to 0.5 RPS, two transient network blips yield a 10% error rate for 2 minutes. Without minimum-sample gating or multi-window burn rates (`1h` + `5m`), on-call gets woken up for a non-incident.

**2. Healthcheck Pollution**: Load balancer `/healthz` probes (every 2s from 20 nodes) inflate Traffic and artificially lower p99 Latency if not excluded via `route!="/healthz"`.

**3. Metric Scrape Gaps**: If a service's `/metrics` endpoint blocks on a slow lock or exceeds Prometheus `scrape_timeout` (default 10s), all four signals go blank right when the service is most saturated.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / From Golden Signals to SLO burn-rate alerting
sections.content:
## From Golden Signals to SLO burn-rate alerting

Raw threshold alerts (`p99 > 500ms`) cause pager fatigue. Instead, convert Latency and Errors into **SLIs** (e.g., `99.9%` of requests `< 300ms` and non-`5xx` over 30 days = `43.2m` monthly error budget) and alert using Google SRE's multi-window burn-rate pattern:

- **Page (Urgent)**: `14.4x` burn rate over both `1h` AND `5m` windows (burns 2% of monthly budget in 1 hour).
- **Page (High)**: `6x` burn rate over both `6h` AND `30m` windows (burns 5% of monthly budget in 6 hours).
- **Ticket (Low)**: `1x`–`3x` burn rate over `3d` / `6h`—investigate during business hours.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Instrument every service with OTel/Prometheus histograms for Latency, splitting `2xx` and `5xx`.
- [ ] Exclude `/healthz` and `/metrics` from Traffic, Latency, and Error SLIs.
- [ ] Bound all metric labels (`service`, `route_template`, `status_class`); ban `user_id` or raw URLs.
- [ ] Monitor Saturation on the tightest bottleneck (DB pool pending, Kafka lag, CPU throttling) using `max()`.
- [ ] Enable Prometheus **exemplars** on latency/error histograms to link directly to distributed traces.
- [ ] Replace static threshold pages with multi-window SLO burn-rate alerts.

interviewProblems.title: Observability Golden Signals
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Observability Golden Signals. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: The Four Golden Signals—Latency, Traffic, Errors, and Saturation—form the minimal, high-signal metric foundation for monitoring any user-facing distributed system. Measuring them with histograms (not averages) and separating successful vs. failed request latencies exposes tail regressions and capacity cliffs before outages hit.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: SLO Burn-Rate Rules applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Grafana + On-Call.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Grafana + On-Call experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Export HDR/Prometheus histograms and compute `histogram_quantile(0.95, ...)` and `0.99` over `rate(...[5m])`.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Instrument every service boundary with Prometheus/OTel histograms for Latency (p50/p95/p99, splitting 2xx from 5xx), Traffic (RPS), Errors (explicit + policy), and Saturation (the tightest resource bottleneck)—and alert on SLO error-budget burn rates rather than raw CPU spikes.
Avoid trap: Computing client-side quantiles (`Summary` metrics) on individual pods and then averaging them across pods in Grafana—quantiles cannot be averaged mathematically.
Avoid trap: Grouping `4xx` client typos (`404`, `400`) into server error alerts, causing noisy pages whenever a bot scrapes invalid URLs.
When to reach for it: Designing baseline SLIs, SLOs, and executive health dashboards for any HTTP, gRPC, or streaming microservice.
When to reach for it: Triaging live incidents to isolate whether degradation stems from downstream latency, traffic surges, code errors, or resource exhaustion.

putItTogether.title: Putting Observability Golden Signals Together
putItTogether.summary: Instrument every service boundary with Prometheus/OTel histograms for Latency (p50/p95/p99, splitting 2xx from 5xx), Traffic (RPS), Errors (explicit + policy), and Saturation (the tightest resource bottleneck)—and alert on SLO error-budget burn rates rather than raw CPU spikes.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Observability Golden Signals before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Splitting `histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)` by `status_class="2xx"` vs. `"5xx"` immediately revealed that `2xx` p99 had actually spiked to 1,800ms on fallback DB queries while `5xx` fast-fails skewed the blended curve.
